newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY UNION-SMITH WARNS WALLABIES COULD STRUGGLE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-SMITH WARNS WALLABIES COULD STRUGGLE.

text.p: Australia rugby union coach Greg Smith on Wednesday said he was worried about facing Five Nations champions France in June because of a lack of preparation.

Smith said the Wallabies could struggle for fluency and cohesion in two home tests against the French in Brisbane and Sydney. "I'm very, very worried -- France are a great team. They are probably right up there with the New Zealand," Smith said.
"I'm given four days to prepare a team to play the European champions and it's just not that easy. It's a gigantic problem."
Smith said the different playing styles of Australia's three provincial sides Queensland, New South Wales and Australian Capital Territory (ACT), made his job of moulding a side harder.
After facing France, Australia will play England, South Africa and New Zealand in a heavy test schedule during the southern hemisphere winter.
Longer term, Smith called on Australian provincial heavyweights Queensland and New South Wales to abandon their current ineffective tactics.
Smith said results in the southern hemisphere Super 12 competition supported his argument in favour of an overhaul.
"New South Wales have won just three (Super 12 matches) and Queensland have won only two out of eight this year so maybe it might be a good idea to have a look at something else," he said.

Australia's reputation has been saved by unheralded Australian Capital Territory (ACT), who are likely to be the country's only representative in the semifinals after lifting themselves to third place in the standings.
In broad terms, ACT employ a faster, running game that brings the backs into play earlier, while New South Wales rely more heavily on the forwards holding possession.
Queensland, in contrast, have traditionally adopted an approach that hinges more on a 10-man kicking game with the emphasis on field position.

Smith said he favoured the New Zealand model in which all provincial sides adopt a similar approach to the All Blacks at test level -- a fast game which emphasises rucking and a quick delivery of the ball at the breakdown.
Australia's three provinces should work together for the benefit of the national team, Smith said.

"I don't have a problem with them playing different games, but we should sit down and talk and formulate something," Smith said. "It works in New Zealand. It hasn't been at the expense of (provincial sides) Auckland or Wellington or Otago."
